paragraphs: Self-Play Preference Optimization, or SPO, trains a policy using comparisons between its own sampled trajectories. A preference or teacher model judges these trajectories, and each trajectory receives a reward based on the fraction of comparisons it wins. This avoids training a separate reward model and gives preference feedback a direct role in policy improvement.

The theoretical foundation is the Minimax Winner, a way of combining preferences through a zero-sum game between policies. The authors use the game's symmetry to show that one agent playing against itself can replace a duel between separately maintained policies while retaining strong convergence guarantees. Their analysis covers preferences that depend on history, contain cycles, or involve randomness.

On continuous control tasks, SPO learns significantly more efficiently than the evaluated reward-model approaches while remaining robust to cyclic and stochastic preferences. The contribution therefore joins a relatively simple training procedure with support for complicated preference patterns. Its guarantees also address the accumulation of errors associated with offline approaches to sequential prediction.
icml-2024-a-minimaximalist-approach-to-r.tldr: SPO uses self-comparisons to train policies without a separate reward model, with guarantees covering complex preferences and encouraging continuous-control results.

paragraphs: Sharpness-aware optimization tries to influence the local shape of the training loss around a model's parameters. This paper argues that concentrating on a few summaries of that shape can be restrictive, particularly for neural networks. Some measures also change dramatically when parameters are rescaled, even when the model has a corresponding parameter invariance.

The authors introduce a family of sharpness measures and associated optimization objectives. They prove an expressiveness result: suitable hyperparameters can represent any function of the training loss Hessian, the matrix describing local curvature. They also show that the objectives explicitly encourage reductions in their corresponding sharpness measures and can support meaningful use with parameter invariances.

Two concrete algorithms illustrate the framework. Frob-SAM targets the Hessian's Frobenius norm, while Det-SAM targets its determinant. These choices capture different aspects of curvature within a common construction. Extensive experiments demonstrate advantages of the framework, complementing the theoretical results. The central contribution is a broader, mathematically characterized design space for sharpness-aware optimization rather than a claim that one curvature measure is universally best.
icml-2024-a-universal-class-of-sharpness.tldr: A universal family of curvature measures yields sharpness-aware objectives, including algorithms targeting the Hessian's Frobenius norm and determinant.

paragraphs: BBox-Adapter addresses task adaptation when a language model is accessible only through an API. In this setting, users may lack access to parameters, embeddings, and even output probabilities, preventing the use of existing fine-tuning methods. The paper introduces a lightweight adapter intended to improve task performance under these access constraints.

Its learning signal separates data from the desired target domain from data belonging to a source domain. Target examples count as positive and source examples as negative. A ranking-based Noise Contrastive Estimation loss encourages target-domain likelihood while discouraging source-domain likelihood. An online mechanism updates this process using positive examples from ground truth, people, or AI feedback, together with negative examples from previous adaptations.

Across the reported tasks and domains, the method improves performance by up to 6.77% and reduces training and inference costs by factors of 31.30 and 1.84, respectively. The performance figure is a reported maximum, not a guaranteed gain for every task. These findings support the adapter as a potentially economical way to adapt models whose internal components are unavailable.
icml-2024-bbox-adapter-lightweight-adapt.tldr: BBox-Adapter uses positive and negative domain examples to adapt API-only language models, reporting performance gains and lower training and inference costs.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether neural networks become easier to interpret when their internal representations use discrete codes. During fine-tuning, vector quantization bottlenecks are inserted at each layer. A hidden representation then becomes the sum of a small number of vectors selected from a larger codebook, replacing a dense continuous state with a sparse selection of reusable components.

The authors first test the approach on a finite state machine dataset with many more hidden states than neurons. Distinct codes represent distinct states, overcoming superposition in this setting. Activating a state's code can make the network behave as though it occupies that state, connecting interpretation to an intervention on behavior.

They also train Transformer language models with up to 410 million parameters on two natural language datasets. The models retain performance with only modest degradation despite the bottleneck. Identified codes capture concepts such as negative emotions and calendar months; activating selected codes can guide topics and pronoun genders during generation. These results suggest codebook features can serve as useful units for both examining and influencing model behavior.
icml-2024-codebook-features-sparse-and-d.tldr: Sparse, discrete codebook features make some neural representations interpretable and controllable while causing only modest performance degradation in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning uses augmented versions of a graph to learn useful node or graph representations. The paper identifies a problem with randomly disrupting graphs: changes can damage community structure, a form of higher-level information. It also argues that augmentation methods focused only on connections or only on node features can leave models vulnerable to different kinds of noise.

The proposed framework learns augmentations while maintaining graph communities. It uses an objective that maximizes spectral changes to bring constraints on graph connections and node features into one framework. Community preservation supplies the structural requirement, while the spectral objective guides the changes made during augmentation.

Experiments across 21 benchmark datasets provide evidence for the framework's advantages and robustness. The findings support community structure as a useful organizing principle when deciding how to alter a graph for learning. The broader contribution is a method for coordinating changes to both topology and features while retaining the group structure that the paper identifies as important for generalization.
icml-2024-community-invariant-graph-cont.tldr: Community-invariant graph contrastive learning coordinates topology and feature augmentations while preserving communities, with benefits demonstrated across 21 datasets.

paragraphs: RNA secondary structure is important for predicting biological function and is more stable and accessible in cells than tertiary structure. The paper addresses the complexity and poor generalization associated with existing deep learning approaches. Its central move is to express secondary structure prediction as a K-Rook problem, turning prediction into probabilistic matching within a finite collection of candidate solutions.

The resulting method, RFold, learns to select the matching solution best suited to an input sequence. To make this manageable, it separates the matching optimization into row-wise and column-wise components. This two-dimensional decomposition reduces the complexity of solving the matching problem while guaranteeing that the produced output satisfies the formulation's validity requirements.

Extensive experiments show competitive predictive performance and inference approximately eight times faster than the compared state-of-the-art approaches. The result connects a simpler mathematical formulation with a practical speed advantage. Output validity and predictive accuracy are separate claims here: the construction guarantees validity, while the experiments provide the evidence that its predictions remain competitive.
icml-2024-deciphering-rna-secondary-stru.tldr: RFold reformulates RNA secondary structure prediction as probabilistic K-Rook matching, delivering valid outputs and competitive accuracy with roughly eightfold faster inference.

paragraphs: DFA-RAG addresses conversations that must follow predetermined response guidelines, such as customer service and emotional support. A language model's ability to generate fluent text does not by itself provide a structured response pathway. The paper introduces an automaton learned from training dialogues to organize how the model moves through a conversation.

This automaton acts as a semantic router. Retrieval selects dialogue examples that fit the current conversational context and supports routing along a deterministic pathway. The framework therefore connects a structured representation of dialogue progression with the examples supplied to the language model, making conversational context part of both routing and response preparation.

The authors emphasize three benefits: a human-readable routing structure, context-sensitive retrieval, and compatibility with existing language models through a plug-and-play design. Extensive benchmarks support the framework's effectiveness. These findings suggest that explicit conversational structure can help guide model responses in settings with established procedures. The stated evidence supports its usefulness as a conversational framework without establishing an unconditional guarantee that every generated response will comply with every guideline.
icml-2024-dfa-rag-conversational-semanti.tldr: DFA-RAG combines a dialogue-derived automaton with contextual example retrieval to guide language models along interpretable conversational pathways.

paragraphs: This paper develops a faster way to apply sampling-based sketches to tensors with two or three modes. A sketch provides a reduced representation for a particular computational task. The authors demonstrate their construction for two classical tasks: zero-norm sampling and producing one-norm embeddings. The focus is the cost of applying these sketches to structured tensor inputs.

The key setting is a rank-one tensor built from vectors of dimension d. Although the corresponding tensor has d squared or d cubed entries, the proposed sketches can be applied in time that scales with d. The stated speed result specifically concerns rank-one inputs and tensors with two or three modes.

The construction uses fast convolution to calculate sums over subsets of tensor entries. Those subsets are sufficiently random for the sampling-based sketches, while their construction makes the sums efficient to compute. This is the central algorithmic contribution: it combines the randomness needed by the sketch with computation that exploits the tensor's structure, avoiding a running time tied to the full number of entries in the stated setting.
icml-2024-fast-sampling-based-sketches-f.tldr: Fast-convolution sampling lets sketches for two- and three-mode rank-one tensors be applied in time scaling with vector dimension rather than tensor size.

paragraphs: FedBPT addresses adapting pretrained language models using data held by different clients. Federated learning allows collaboration without collecting that data in one central location, but ordinary model fine-tuning can require expensive computation, substantial communication, and access to model parameters. These requirements become difficult when a model is available only through an inference interface.

The framework trains prompts while allowing clients to treat the language model as a black-box API. It uses gradient-free optimization, so adaptation does not depend on obtaining gradients from the underlying model. Focusing on prompts also reduces the number of variables exchanged during collaboration, targeting communication, computation, and storage costs together.

Experiments report substantial reductions in communication and memory use while retaining competitive task performance. This makes the result relevant to settings where client resources and model access are both constrained. Its privacy-oriented contribution is collaborative adaptation without centralized data collection, combined with a lightweight optimization target. The findings support prompt tuning as a practical route to federated language-model adaptation under the tested conditions.
icml-2024-fedbpt-efficient-federated-bla.tldr: FedBPT combines federated learning with gradient-free prompt tuning to adapt API-accessible language models with substantially lower communication and memory costs.

paragraphs: Clustering groups records for later analysis, so users often need to understand which features drive those groups. This paper introduces a deep learning framework for tabular data that predicts cluster assignments and identifies influential features. It addresses interpretation at two levels: the individual record and the cluster containing many records.

First, a self-supervised procedure identifies a subset of informative features for each data point. A further model predicts assignments and produces a gate matrix that selects features at the cluster level. Together, these components provide information about what drives an individual assignment and which features characterize a broader group.

The authors evaluate the framework on tabular datasets from biology, text, images, and physics. They report reliable cluster predictions and assess interpretation using previously proposed metrics at both sample and cluster levels. The contribution is therefore a clustering procedure that makes feature selection part of the model's output. This can give practitioners more specific information for examining their groups than cluster labels alone, with empirical evidence across the reported domains.
icml-2024-interpretable-deep-clustering-.tldr: This framework clusters tabular records while identifying the features driving individual assignments and entire clusters.

paragraphs: Graph representation learning converts graphs into vectors that can support tasks such as classification. This paper focuses on making those representations diverse and informative. It introduces graph entropy as the quantity to maximize, defining a probability distribution using both the representations of individual nodes and a representation of the whole graph.

Directly computing this entropy is NP-hard because its definition involves a difficult vertex-packing polytope. The authors address that obstacle with an approximation based on orthonormal representations. This makes entropy maximization usable as a learning approach without requiring direct solution of the original hard computation.

The method is implemented with graph neural networks and produces representations at both node and graph levels. Experiments compare it with many baselines in unsupervised and semi-supervised tasks and demonstrate its effectiveness. The significance is the connection between an explicit information-based objective and practical representation learning. The approximation is central to that connection: it makes a theoretically motivated but computationally difficult measure useful for training models in the evaluated settings.
icml-2024-learning-graph-representation-.tldr: An approximation to graph entropy maximization trains graph neural networks to produce informative node and graph representations.

paragraphs: Learning rapidly varying functions from low-dimensional inputs is important in tasks such as view synthesis and time-series regression. Fourier-feature positional encodings help with this problem, but their frequency choices often require manual adjustment for each task. Existing encodings can also struggle to learn high-frequency functions efficiently when data is limited.

The paper introduces sinusoidal positional encoding, or SPE, to learn adaptive frequency features that closely match the underlying function. Frequency adaptation is the central design goal: the representation should adjust to the function being learned instead of depending on a manually selected set of Fourier features. SPE is designed as a direct replacement for existing positional encodings.

Across experiments in 3D view synthesis, text-to-speech generation, and one-dimensional regression, SPE achieves better fidelity and faster training without hyperparameter tuning. These are empirical results across the evaluated tasks. The combination of adaptive features and a drop-in implementation matters because it offers improvements at a component already used in many learning systems, with less task-specific adjustment in the reported experiments.
icml-2024-learning-high-frequency-functi.tldr: SPE learns adaptive frequency features as a drop-in positional encoding, improving fidelity and training speed without hyperparameter tuning in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Visual model-based reinforcement learning uses observations to learn a world model that supports decision-making. Irrelevant visual changes can interfere with this process: the model may represent distracting details instead of the aspects of the environment needed for the task. The paper targets this problem in visually complex control settings.

The approach combines masking across space and time, a bisimulation principle, and reconstruction in the latent representation. These components aim to preserve task-specific aspects of the environment while removing nonessential information. The authors also address instability that can arise when representations, environment dynamics, and the policy are trained together, introducing a Hybrid Recurrent State-Space Model to improve representation robustness.

The empirical evaluation reports significant improvements over existing methods on several visually complex control tasks. These include Maniskill tasks with external distractors from the Matterport environment. The findings support the value of learning a world representation that resists irrelevant observation changes. The contribution combines a strategy for selecting task-relevant information with a model structure intended to make policy learning more stable.
icml-2024-learning-latent-dynamic-robust.tldr: Masking, bisimulation, latent reconstruction, and a hybrid state-space model improve world-model learning in visually distracting control environments.

paragraphs: LSEnet addresses graph clustering when the number of clusters is unknown. Many deep clustering methods require that number beforehand, making it an input to the method rather than something discovered from the graph. The paper approaches this challenge through structural information, an information-theoretic description of graph organization.

The authors develop a continuous, differentiable form of structural information and provide theoretical results for it. Minimizing this quantity constructs an optimal partitioning tree in which densely connected nodes tend to receive the same assignment. They also establish it as a graph clustering objective that does not require a predefined cluster count.

LSEnet implements this approach in the Lorentz model of hyperbolic space. Its graph convolution operates on that geometry and incorporates node features into the structural information framework. Experiments on real graphs report superiority over the evaluated alternatives. The contribution brings together an objective for discovering cluster structure, a differentiable formulation suitable for deep learning, and a neural architecture that uses both graph connections and node attributes.
icml-2024-lsenet-lorentz-structural-entr.tldr: LSEnet combines differentiable structural information with hyperbolic graph learning to cluster graphs without a predefined number of clusters.

paragraphs: This paper examines how two-layer neural networks learn features by studying the kernel induced by their first layer. The analysis uses a mean-field regime and a two-timescale limit in which the second layer changes much faster than the first. Under that setup, training becomes an optimization problem over the network's intrinsic kernel.

The authors prove global convergence for the resulting mean-field Langevin dynamics. They also derive errors associated with discretizing time and representing the dynamics with a finite number of particles. These results connect the limiting mathematical description with approximations needed to represent its evolution computationally.

The analysis further shows that, in the studied setting, two-layer networks can learn a union of multiple reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces more efficiently than kernel methods. The learned kernel depends on the data and aligns with the target function. A separate label-noise procedure also converges to a global optimum, with degrees of freedom appearing as implicit regularization. Together, these results describe feature learning as adaptive kernel learning under the paper's specified limiting assumptions.
icml-2024-mean-field-analysis-on-two-lay.tldr: Under a two-timescale mean-field limit, two-layer networks learn adaptive kernels with global convergence guarantees and characterized discretization errors.

paragraphs: Machine teaching asks how many examples a teacher needs to communicate a concept to a learner. This paper studies a particular model in which a size function on concepts and examples determines the teacher mapping. The quantity of interest is the teaching dimension: the minimum example requirement needed to handle any concept in the class.

The authors prove a conjecture identifying the worst case as a function of the number of concepts. That worst case occurs when the consistency matrix contains the binary representations of consecutive numbers starting at zero. The result gives a specific combinatorial arrangement that attains the hardest teaching requirement within the model.

The proof connects this teaching question to the geometry of hypercubes. The authors describe their theorem as a generalization of a result resolving the hypercube edge-isoperimetry problem and base their argument on an existing combinatorial lemma. The contribution is an exact theoretical characterization of the worst case for this teaching model, giving the previously conjectured binary arrangement a proven extremal role.
icml-2024-on-a-combinatorial-problem-ari.tldr: The paper proves which binary consistency-matrix arrangement gives the worst teaching dimension in a size-based machine-teaching model.

paragraphs: Online anomaly detection needs a threshold that decides when an observation should trigger an alert. Choosing that threshold is especially difficult without supervision and when the incoming data distribution changes. This paper connects threshold selection to the construction of confidence sequences, bringing a statistical framework into the process of updating thresholds over time.

The proposed algorithm adapts its threshold online and is designed to remain robust to distribution shifts. The authors establish guarantees on both false positives and false negatives without imposing distributional assumptions. These two kinds of error correspond to raising an alert unnecessarily and failing to flag an anomaly, so the theory addresses both sides of threshold selection.

The algorithm can also begin with offline data. Relevant historical data improves performance, while irrelevant historical data causes only bounded degradation. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show better performance than commonly used baselines. Together, the results support an approach that combines ongoing adaptation, statistical error guarantees, and a controlled way to benefit from information available before monitoring begins.
icml-2024-online-adaptive-anomaly-thresh.tldr: Confidence-sequence-based thresholding adapts to distribution shifts, provides false-positive and false-negative guarantees, and can safely benefit from relevant historical data.

paragraphs: Online algorithms must make decisions before all relevant information is available. Predictions can help, but their reliability matters. This paper studies how algorithms should use predictions accompanied by uncertainty information, specifically a stated likelihood that the true value lies within a particular range. The objective is to use that additional information effectively at decision time.

The authors investigate two classic online problems, ski rental and online search. Their results show that fully exploiting uncertainty-quantified predictions requires substantial changes to algorithm design. Providing an uncertainty range is therefore only part of the solution; the decision rule must be designed to make use of what that range says about possible outcomes.

The paper also considers more general forms of uncertainty quantification through an online learning framework for repeated problem instances. This framework learns how to use uncertainty information when making decisions across instances. The contribution connects predictive uncertainty with online decision-making at two levels: algorithms for particular problems and a learning approach that can adapt its use of uncertainty over repeated decisions.
icml-2024-online-algorithms-with-uncerta.tldr: Online algorithms can use quantified predictive uncertainty, but doing so effectively requires redesigned decision rules and, across repeated instances, learning how to exploit it.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization uses an acquisition function to choose which candidate to evaluate next. This paper studies the theoretical and practical behavior of several such rules, focusing on Bayesian cumulative regret. A recent randomized version of Gaussian process upper confidence bound had obtained a tighter regret bound, motivating the authors to investigate whether other approaches achieve it.

They first prove that Thompson sampling also satisfies this tighter bound. They then analyze PIMS, an acquisition function based on probability of improvement relative to the maximum of a sampled function path. PIMS receives the same tighter regret guarantee and avoids the hyperparameter tuning associated with the GP-UCB acquisition rule.

The practical motivation is that GP-UCB can require manual tuning, while Thompson sampling can explore excessively. A broad set of experiments supports PIMS as a way to mitigate these issues. The paper therefore contributes both a stronger analysis of an established sampling method and a theoretically supported alternative whose evaluation addresses practical difficulties in selecting where to sample next.
icml-2024-posterior-sampling-based-bayes.tldr: Thompson sampling and PIMS receive tighter Bayesian regret bounds, while PIMS also reduces acquisition-rule tuning and mitigates over-exploration in experiments.

paragraphs: This paper examines why different approaches to preference-based language-model fine-tuning can produce conflicting results. It compares techniques through rigorous analysis on simplified problems and full-scale language-model tasks. The aim is to identify which properties of a training procedure matter, including where its responses come from and how it changes their probabilities.

The main finding favors approaches that sample from the current policy and reduce the likelihood of certain responses. Sampling from the current policy supplies on-policy data; explicitly pushing probabilities downward supplies a negative gradient. In the studied problems, approaches using these properties outperform offline methods and maximum-likelihood objectives.

The authors explain the results using mode-seeking objectives for categorical distributions. These objectives can change probability mass on particular categories faster than maximum likelihood, enabling more effective redistribution among responses. This connects the value of suboptimal responses to the learning update: such responses can supply useful evidence about what to suppress. The analysis offers guidance for both preference-training objectives and data collection, grounded in the settings examined.
icml-2024-preference-fine-tuning-of-llms.tldr: The analysis favors preference fine-tuning that samples current-model responses and actively lowers the probability of undesirable ones.

paragraphs: This paper studies linear regression with multiple outcomes when learners can observe only some components of both the inputs and outputs. Missing information affects the quantities used to predict and the quantities being predicted. The authors develop algorithms specifically for this partially observed, multivariate setting.

The proposed methods use squared-error and absolute-error losses, with ridge-like and Lasso-type penalties as described in the formulation. The authors establish error bounds for all of their algorithms. The squared-error methods additionally have probably approximately correct guarantees, a property that the paper distinguishes from its absolute-error results.

Numerical experiments show improvements over applying existing single-outcome algorithms separately to each output coordinate. This supports treating the multivariate problem with methods designed for its observation constraints. The experiments also indicate that absolute-error loss or a Lasso-type penalty can improve predictions in the presence of outliers or high-dimensional features. These are conditional advantages: the appropriate loss and penalty depend on the data characteristics, while the theoretical results distinguish the guarantees available for the different methods.
icml-2024-regression-learning-with-limit.tldr: New regression algorithms handle partially observed inputs and multiple outputs, with error bounds and empirical benefits over fitting each output separately.

paragraphs: A reachability specification asks a reinforcement-learning agent to eventually visit a target set. Although learning from this kind of objective has produced strong empirical results, general probably approximately correct guarantees are impossible in the setting motivating the paper. The authors investigate what additional information makes such a guarantee possible.

They consider providing the learner with expected conditional distance information, abbreviated ECD. Their lower-bound results establish the necessity of this information for PAC guarantees in the studied problem. They also construct an algorithm that achieves a PAC guarantee when ECD information is supplied, providing a positive result alongside the lower bounds.

The contribution identifies an information requirement that changes what can be guaranteed about reachability learning. The authors describe their method as the first such approach, to their knowledge, that learns policies without assumptions on the underlying environment. That statement accompanies an explicit requirement: the learner receives ECD information. The result therefore links a theoretical impossibility to an achievable learning guarantee through a specified addition to what the learner knows.
icml-2024-reinforcement-learning-from-re.tldr: Expected conditional distance information enables PAC-guaranteed reachability learning, with lower bounds establishing its necessity in the studied setting.

paragraphs: Some probability distributions remain unchanged under a family of transformations. This paper asks how that invariance can reduce the data required to estimate differences between distributions. The mathematical setting covers smooth actions of Lie groups on manifolds, allowing the analysis to include both finite groups and groups with positive dimension.

The authors derive sample-complexity results for the 1-Wasserstein distance, Sobolev integral probability metrics, and maximum mean discrepancy. They also study density estimation under two error measures. The results identify a multiplicative improvement related to group size for finite groups, or to the normalized volume of the quotient space for positive-dimensional groups.

For groups of positive dimension, the gains also include an improvement in the exponent of the convergence rate. This means the benefit affects how estimation error decreases with additional samples, alongside the multiplicative factor. The paper extends existing bounds for finite group actions and presents new results for positive-dimensional groups. Its contribution is a quantitative account of how the stated distributional invariances can make several estimation problems statistically easier.
icml-2024-sample-complexity-bounds-for-e.tldr: Distributional invariances improve sample-complexity bounds for divergence and density estimation, including faster convergence-rate exponents for positive-dimensional groups.

paragraphs: Reliable labels can be expensive to obtain, while several imperfect sources may be readily available. This paper studies learning from multiple noisy label sources, such as rule-based supervision. It focuses on what the authors call self-cognition: a neural network's ability to distinguish noise during its own training.

The theoretical analysis identifies two levels of this ability. A network can recognize noise attached to individual examples within one source and distinguish the quality of different sources. These are complementary judgments, since identifying an unreliable label and recognizing an unreliable source operate at different levels of the supervision.

The authors turn these insights into Self-cognitive Denoising for Multiple noisy label sources, or SDM. The method uses the network's noise-recognition ability to denoise during training, and a selective distillation module improves computational efficiency. Experiments on several datasets demonstrate advantages over the evaluated alternatives. The contribution connects a theoretical account of noise recognition with a training method that uses both example-level and source-level information when learning from imperfect supervision.
icml-2024-self-cognitive-denoising-in-th.tldr: SDM uses neural networks' ability to recognize noisy examples and unreliable label sources to denoise training, with selective distillation improving efficiency.

paragraphs: video-SALMONN is an end-to-end model for understanding videos through visual frames, audio events, music, and speech. The paper emphasizes speech as an understudied part of audio-visual language modeling. Speech requires fine temporal detail, creating a need to preserve timing information while processing the other video elements efficiently.

A multi-resolution causal Q-Former connects pretrained audio-visual encoders to the backbone language model. Its design addresses that balance between detailed speech information and efficient handling of other content. The training procedure adds a diversity loss and mixed training with unpaired audio and visual data to prevent particular frames or a single modality from dominating learning.

On the paper's introduced benchmark, video-SALMONN reports absolute accuracy improvements exceeding 25 percentage points for video question answering and 30 percentage points for audio-visual questions involving human speech. The authors also report comprehension and reasoning abilities on tasks they describe as unprecedented for other audio-visual language models. These findings support combining speech-sensitive temporal processing with training that encourages the model to use multiple sources of information.
icml-2024-video-salmonn-speech-enhanced-.tldr: video-SALMONN integrates speech, sound, music, and frames, reporting large absolute accuracy improvements on its audio-visual question-answering benchmark.
